prompt: A Deployment apply succeeds. Its generation is 18, observedGeneration is 16, no new ReplicaSet exists, existing Pods are Ready and users still receive the old version. Diagnose the boundary and give a safe response.
directAnswer: The API accepted current intent, but the Deployment controller status and children have not reached generation 18. Bind cluster/context/identity and Deployment UID, preserve generation/resourceVersion/managedFields, then inspect controller leader Lease, list-watch/API access, queue age/retries/errors, field conflicts, admission and owned ReplicaSets. Existing Ready Pods correctly serve old intent and do not prove the new rollout happened. Repair the controller/API dependency rather than patching status or creating a ReplicaSet manually. Verify observedGeneration 18, the correct new ReplicaSet owner UID/template, Pod placement/readiness, Service endpoints and user version before closure.
foundation: API persistence, controller observation and workload/user convergence are separate asynchronous stages.
reasoningSteps: Bind exact cluster, namespace, Deployment name and UID.
Confirm apply response, audit ID, generation, resourceVersion and field manager.
Compare generation with observedGeneration and read conditions.
List ReplicaSets and owner UIDs; prove the new desired template has no child.
Identify Deployment controller leader and process health.
Inspect watch continuity, queue depth/age, retries, errors and API write access.
Check server-side apply conflicts and admission/API/etcd latency.
Repair the owning loop or dependency without mutating status/children.
Verify current-generation ownership chain, scheduling, readiness, endpoints and user version.
Add stall detection based on generation lag and reconcile age.
seniorAnswer: I classify this after API persistence and before Deployment reconciliation. Ready old Pods explain availability, not rollout success. I freeze further changes, bind UID and field ownership, and inspect the controller leader, watch/cache, queue and API writes. I do not patch observedGeneration or hand-create children. Recovery restores the controller path; success requires the generation-18 ReplicaSet with correct owner/template, healthy Pods, endpoint revision and a user request showing the new version.
weakAnswer: Delete the old Pods so Kubernetes recreates them with the new version.
whyWeak: The old ReplicaSet still owns the old template, so deletion recreates old Pods while hiding the stalled Deployment controller and risking availability.

evidence.proves: Reported Deployment status does not cover current desired generation.

evidence.doesNotProve: Whether watch, queue, conflict or API write caused it.

evidence.proves: Old owned workload currently reports readiness.
evidence.doesNotProve: New version rollout or user correctness.

followUps.answer: It is controller-owned observation; patching hides the failure and creates false status.
Age of a nonzero generation-observedGeneration mismatch plus controller queue/reconcile signals.
Only through the owning Deployment/ReplicaSet rollout and disruption policy, not as speculative controller repair.

rubric.observableEvidence: Separates API acceptance from Deployment reconciliation.
Uses UID, generations, RV and ownership.
Checks leader, watch, queue, errors and writes.
Checks child, Pod, endpoint and user revision.
